analysis.one_liner: Repeals the new lower tax rates that the 2017 tax law created for profits US companies keep overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; with 21 Democratic sponsors, it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law created two new ways for US multinational companies to pay lower taxes on profits earned from intangible assets like patents, trademarks, and software held abroad. This bill would repeal both breaks entirely, starting with the 2018 tax year. That would raise revenue from multinational corporations and remove a tax incentive to shift jobs and profits overseas.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the roughly $100 billion a year in revenue the two breaks are estimated to give up is instead used for public services or to reduce deficits that otherwise pressure future spending. Workers whose jobs compete with offshored work also benefit, since the lower rate rewards companies for locating intangible assets and the profits they generate in low-tax foreign countries.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 250 of the tax code, eliminating the reduced tax rate on foreign-derived intangible income and the global intangible low-taxed income regime, effective for tax years after 2017 [S3] [S2].
Without the breaks, US companies would pay closer to the standard 21% corporate rate on those foreign profits rather than the reduced effective rates created by the 2017 law [S2].
The bill's stated purpose is to eliminate tax preferences for foreign profits, removing a structure that rewards keeping jobs and intangible assets offshore [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations — especially tech, pharmaceutical, and other companies whose value comes from patents, software, and brands held abroad — would pay billions more in taxes each year. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers or shareholders, and supporters of the 2017 rates argued the breaks helped US companies compete with foreign rivals.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to income earned abroad by US multinationals; critics of repeal argue that raising their tax rate puts them at a disadvantage against foreign competitors who pay their home country's lower rates [S3].

Repealing the breaks adds billions in annual taxes on corporations, some portion of which economists expect to show up in consumer prices or shareholder returns rather than coming entirely out of corporate profits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would close two loopholes created just months earlier, recovering substantial revenue from companies that book intangible-asset profits in low-tax countries. The main cost falls on multinationals and potentially on shareholders and some consumers through higher prices. For ordinary households the benefit is indirect — revenue for public priorities rather than a check in the mail — but the bill would also remove a tax structure that rewards moving work offshore.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 1, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1] [S5].
Twenty Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after the referral to committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations keep the reduced rates on foreign intangible income that the bill would have repealed, because the bill never advanced past its committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: US multinationals keep the tax breaks

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors were Democrats; the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations (especially tech and pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: These companies benefit from the reduced rates on foreign intangible income that the bill repeals; the breaks are worth billions a year and reward booking patents and software profits in low-tax countries. Their gain under the status quo is revenue the government does not collect.
